505.title: Many names for a bowl
505.hook: don't insist on your local word; a bowl has many names
505.howItsDone: Buddhist teachings are chanted and studied in Pali, Sanskrit, Chinese, Tibetan, Japanese, English and other languages; a Vinaya passage on learning the Buddha's words in one's own dialect is read differently by different schools and scholars.

segments.voice: Yesterday: forty tabs and a pleasant fog, and a mind not scattered, not stuck. Your line: neither flies off nor holds on.

Soda. Pop. Coke, even when it isn't. Sneakers or tennis shoes. Some people have argued about these words at a family reunion with real heat. The hundred and thirty-ninth discourse is about living without conflict, and much of it is about big things: pleasure and self-torment, praise and blame, how to speak. But tucked inside is a small, almost funny example about tableware. The same simple bowl, the Buddha notices, goes by different names in different districts. And he has something to say about people who insist theirs is the real one.
screen: `SODA. POP. COKE.` → `A DISCOURSE ON NON-CONFLICT.` → `ONE BOWL, MANY NAMES.`

segments.voice: The discourse is called the exposition of non-conflict, araṇa. It lists ways to live without stirring up conflict. Don't pursue sensual pleasure, and don't torment yourself: the middle way. Know what praise and blame are, and teach without either. Don't say things in secret that would hurt if known, or speak harshly to someone's face. Speak unhurriedly, because hurried speech tires the body and the mind, and is hard to follow. And: don't insist on local language, and don't override ordinary usage. Here's the example. In one district, people call a bowl pati. In another, patta. In others, still other names. Someone who clings to their own district's word says: only this is correct, everything else is wrong. That, the text says, is insisting on local language and overriding ordinary usage, a path with conflict in it. The other person, wherever they go, thinks: it seems these people call it this. And speaks as they do, without grasping. That's the path without conflict. A teaching about freedom stops to talk about kitchen words, and it fits. Some fights aren't about the thing at all; they're about whose name for it wins. The monastic rules have a related passage, and readers disagree about it: some hear the Buddha letting monks learn his words in their own dialects; the old commentary hears his own language. A bowl holds rice whatever it's called. The text ends by naming a monk, Subhuti, as one who walked this way of non-conflict.
screen: `ARANA: THE WAY OF NON-CONFLICT` · `SPEAK UNHURRIEDLY` · `PATI, PATTA, AND MORE` · `SPEAK AS THEY DO` · then, large: `MANY NAMES FOR A BOWL.`

segments.voice: Think of a word, a name or a pronunciation you've corrected someone about, or wanted to: a term for God, a holiday, a dish. Picture them saying it their way, notice any little push to fix it, and let the push soften: it seems they call it this. Let the breath be unhurried.
Arana. Without conflict: don't insist your local word, like pati or patta, is the only right one; speak as people speak, without grasping. Today's word.
Your line: speak as people speak. Pati or patta, it's still a bowl. Day five hundred five, done.

screen: `DAY 505 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE STRANGER WAS THE TEACHER.`

506.title: The stranger was the teacher
506.hook: Pukkusati meets the Buddha in a potter's shed without knowing him, and is taught the six elements
506.howItsDone: The six-element contemplation of MN 140 is taught in Theravada and other meditation traditions, with practitioners reviewing earth, water, fire, air, space and consciousness in the body and seeing each as not-self.

segments.voice: Yesterday: arana, non-conflict, and a bowl called pati in one place and patta in another. Your line: speak as people speak.

Evening, on the road near Rajagaha. A wandering monk asks a potter named Bhaggava if he can spend the night in his workshop. The potter says: fine by me, but someone's already staying there. Ask him. Inside is a man who has left home for the homeless life out of faith in a teacher he has never met. His name is Pukkusati. The traveler asks: may I stay? Pukkusati says: the workshop is roomy. Stay as you like. He has no idea who just walked in.
screen: `A POTTER'S WORKSHOP AT EVENING.` → `PUKKUSATI, FAITHFUL, NEVER MET HIM.` → `A TRAVELER ASKS TO STAY.`

segments.voice: They sit through most of the night. Then the traveler asks: on whose account did you go forth? Who's your teacher? Pukkusati answers: the recluse Gotama, the Sakyan. Have you seen him? Would you recognize him? No, says Pukkusati. I've never seen him. If I saw him, I wouldn't know him. The Buddha doesn't reveal himself. He thinks: this young man went forth on my account. Let me teach him. A person, he says, is made of six elements: earth, water, fire, air, space and consciousness. The solid in the body is earth, and so is the solid outside it. Seeing that, you see: this is not mine, this is not me, this is not my self. Same for water, fire, air and space. Then what remains is consciousness, and then a pure, bright equanimity, like gold refined by a goldsmith until it's soft and shining. Even that, he says, is conditioned, and he shows how to let go of it too. When the teaching ends, Pukkusati understands who's speaking. He bows and asks forgiveness for calling the Buddha friend, like an equal. The Buddha accepts. Pukkusati asks for full ordination, and is told he needs a bowl and robes. He goes to find them, and on the way, the text says, a stray cow kills him. The Buddha tells the monks Pukkusati had already gone far, beyond returning to this world. He had found his teacher, for one night, without knowing it.
screen: `HAVE YOU SEEN HIM?` · `SIX ELEMENTS: NOT MINE, NOT ME` · `GOLD REFINED TO SHINING` · `HE KNOWS, AND BOWS` · then, large: `THE STRANGER WAS THE TEACHER.`

segments.voice: Feel the solid in you: earth; the moist: water; the warmth: fire; the breath moving: air; the spaces in mouth and ears: space; and the knowing of it all: consciousness. Then think of someone you'll meet whom you don't really know, a cashier, a driver, a new colleague, and leave a little room for the possibility that they have something to teach you.
Dhatu. Element: Pukkusati spent a night in a potter's shed with the Buddha, not knowing him, and was taught the six elements, or dhatus. Today's word.
Your line: found his teacher without knowing. A roomy workshop, and a door left open. See you tomorrow.

507.title: The truths expounded
507.hook: Sariputta sets out the four truths in detail
507.howItsDone: The four noble truths are taught in Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana schools alike, and the detailed analysis in MN 141 has a close parallel in the Digha Nikaya's great discourse on the foundations of mindfulness (DN 22).

segments.voice: Yesterday: dhatu, the six elements, taught to Pukkusati in a potter's shed. Your line: found his teacher without knowing.

The Deer Park at Isipatana, near Benares: in the tradition, the place where the Buddha first taught the four noble truths to five companions. In the hundred and forty-first discourse, he's there again. He reminds the monks that the wheel of the teaching was first set rolling right here, by announcing four truths. Then he does something a good teacher does. He points to two students. Go to Sariputta and Moggallana, he says. Learn from them. And he goes into his dwelling.
screen: `THE DEER PARK, NEAR BENARES.` → `WHERE THE WHEEL FIRST ROLLED.` → `GO TO SARIPUTTA AND MOGGALLANA.`

segments.voice: Before he leaves, the Buddha gives a picture of his two chief students. Sariputta is like a mother who gives birth; Moggallana, like a nurse who raises the child. Sariputta trains people to the first real breakthrough. Moggallana trains them to the highest goal. So Sariputta addresses the monks and does what the title says: he expounds. He takes each truth and opens it. First, suffering. Birth is suffering, and he defines birth, the coming into being of beings. Aging is suffering: gray hair, wrinkled skin, failing faculties. Death, sorrow, grief, despair, each named and described. Not getting what you want is suffering. And in short, the five heaps that are clung to are suffering. Second, the origin: craving that leads to renewed being, craving for pleasure, for becoming, for non-becoming. Third, the cessation: the complete fading and ending of that craving, letting it go. Fourth, the path, and he defines each of the eight factors one by one, from right view, knowing these four truths, to right concentration. Nothing dramatic happens. No one is suddenly freed in the story. It's a careful lecture, almost a textbook, and that's the point. The four truths can be announced in a minute, as the Buddha did at the start. But they're meant to be unfolded, slowly, word by word, by students who've learned them well enough to teach. Expounded means laid out, line by line, so others can walk through it.
screen: `A MOTHER AND A NURSE` · `SUFFERING, DEFINED WORD BY WORD` · `CRAVING, ITS ENDING, THE PATH` · `ANNOUNCED, THEN UNFOLDED` · then, large: `EXPOUNDED.`

segments.voice: In your own words, slowly, say one line with each out-breath: there is suffering; it has a cause, craving; it can end; there is a path. Then go around again, and let each line touch something real from your week: a small ache, a want, a moment of ease, a step you took.
Sacca. Truth: at the Deer Park, Sariputta lays out the four noble truths, the ariya saccas, in detail, defining each one word by word. Today's word.
Your line: expounded. Four short truths, opened one word at a time. That's day five hundred seven.

508.title: The robe gift
508.hook: Mahapajapati offers a robe she made; the kinds of offering
508.howItsDone: In Theravada countries the Kathina ceremony at the end of the rains retreat is a major occasion when lay people offer robe cloth to the monastic community as a whole, rather than to one monk.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sacca, the four truths, expounded by Sariputta word by word. Your line: expounded.

A sweater someone knitted for you. It took them weeks. It's a little lopsided, and you'd never give it away. The hundred and forty-second discourse begins with a gift like that. The Buddha is back among the Sakyans, at Kapilavatthu. Mahapajapati Gotami, his mother's sister, the woman who raised him after his mother died, comes to him with a new robe cloth. She spun the thread herself. She wove it herself. This is for you, Lord, she says. Please accept it out of compassion. And the Buddha says no.
screen: `A HAND-KNITTED SWEATER.` → `SPUN AND WOVEN BY HER OWN HANDS.` → `THE BUDDHA SAYS: GIVE IT TO THE SANGHA.`

segments.voice: Give it to the community, Gotami, he says. When you give to the community, both I and the community are honored. She asks again. He says the same. A third time. Then Ananda steps in, gently. Lord, please accept it. She was so helpful to you: your mother's sister, your nurse, your foster mother. When your mother died, she gave you her own milk. And the Buddha has helped her too, Ananda adds: through him she found refuge and the precepts. The Buddha agrees that each has helped the other, and that such debts can't be easily repaid with robes or food. Then he turns the moment into a teaching about giving. He lists fourteen kinds of personal gifts, from a gift to a Buddha down to a gift to an animal. Even a gift to an animal, he says, can be expected to repay a hundredfold. Then seven kinds of gifts to the community. And four ways a gift is made pure: by the giver, by the receiver, by both, or by neither, depending on whose conduct is good. Why refuse his foster mother? The discourse doesn't explain in a single line, and it doesn't say what happened to the robe. One common reading: he wanted her gift to reach as many people as it could, and to grow her merit beyond one person. A later commentary tells its own story of where the robe went. What's clear is the gift itself: thread spun by hand, for someone loved, and a teaching about generosity that grew from it.
screen: `GIVE IT TO THE COMMUNITY` · `ANANDA: SHE NURSED YOU` · `FOURTEEN GIFTS, FOUR PURITIES` · `A GIFT MADE TO REACH FAR` · then, large: `MADE BY HAND.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you could give a small thing made by your own hands: a note written out, not typed; a meal; a drawing; a repaired thing. Picture making it, and notice the care that goes in before anyone receives it, because that's part of the gift too. Then rest with the breath, and if you like, let the idea grow into a plan.
Dakkhina. An offering, a gift given with respect: Mahapajapati's handmade robe, which the Buddha asked her to give to the whole community, and the teaching on giving that followed. Today's word.
Your line: made by hand. Thread spun for one person became a teaching on giving for everyone. Until tomorrow.

509.title: Anathapindika's last days
509.hook: dying, the great giver is taught not to cling to anything, and weeps at its depth
509.howItsDone: Buddhist monks and friends visit the sick and the dying to chant and to recall teachings on non-clinging; MN 143 shows Sariputta doing exactly that.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dakkhina, Mahapajapati's handmade robe, and a teaching on giving. Your line: made by hand.

Anathapindika's name, tradition says, means the one who gives food to the unprotected. He's the merchant who, in the tradition, bought Jeta's Grove for the Buddha by covering the ground with coins. Again and again this year, a discourse has opened in the park he gave. Now he is very ill. He sends a man to pay his respects to the Buddha, and then to Sariputta with a request: please come, out of compassion. Sariputta comes, with Ananda, and asks how he is. The answer is honest: the pain is getting worse, not better.
screen: `THE ONE WHO FEEDS THE UNPROTECTED.` → `THE GIVER OF JETA'S GROVE.` → `THE PAIN IS GETTING WORSE.`

segments.voice: He describes it plainly, in the text's images: like a strong man splitting his head with a sharp sword, like a tight strap around the head, like a butcher's knife in the belly, like being held over hot coals. Sariputta doesn't offer comfort first. He offers a training. Train like this, householder: I won't cling to the eye, and my consciousness won't depend on the eye. Not to the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, the mind. Not to sights, sounds, smells, tastes, touches or thoughts. Not to the elements, not to the five heaps. Not to this world, and my consciousness won't depend on this world. Not to any world beyond. Not to anything seen, heard, sensed, known, sought or explored. Line after line, everything a dying person might hold. And Anathapindika weeps. Ananda asks: are you sinking, householder? No, he says. I've served the Teacher and the monks for so long, and I've never heard a talk like this. Sariputta answers that such talks are usually given to monastics, not to lay people. Before they go, Anathapindika asks for something. Let talks like this be given to lay people too. There are those with little dust in their eyes who will be lost if they never hear it. Soon after they leave, he dies. The text says he was reborn among the gods, and came back one night to Jeta's Grove, glowing, to praise it and Sariputta. The great giver's last gift was a request: share this with everyone.

segments.voice: Choose one small thing you're holding today: a plan, an opinion, a worry about tomorrow, a feeling about yourself. Your line: not clinging to this. A dying man's last request was that teachings like this reach lay people too. Go gently.

510.title: Punna goes west
510.hook: to a fierce land: if they insult me, I'll think them kind for not hitting me
510.howItsDone: Punna's answers are taught as an example of patience (khanti), which Theravada counts among the perfections (parami) a practitioner develops.

segments.voice: Yesterday: upadana, and Sariputta's teaching on not clinging, given to a dying giver. Your line: not clinging to this.

A new job, a new city, a team with a reputation. Everyone warns you: they're rough over there. You'll get eaten alive. The hundred and forty-fifth discourse starts with a monk named Punna asking the Buddha for a short teaching before he leaves. The Buddha gives it, then asks: where will you live? Punna names a region to the west called Sunaparanta. The Buddha says, plainly: the people there are fierce, Punna. They're rough. What will you do if they insult you?
screen: `THEY'RE ROUGH OVER THERE.` → `PUNNA NAMES THE WEST.` → `WHAT IF THEY INSULT YOU?`

segments.voice: The short teaching comes first. If you delight in what you see, hear, smell, taste, touch and think, and hold on to it, suffering comes. If you don't, it ends. Then the conversation, like a ladder going down. If they insult you? Punna: I'll think, these people are good, really good, since they don't hit me with their fists. And if they hit you? At least they don't throw clods of earth at me. And if they do? At least they don't beat me with a stick. And if they do? At least they don't use a knife. The Buddha keeps going, all the way to the worst, and Punna's answer never turns to hate. Even facing the end of his life, he answers calmly. Good, Punna, the Buddha says. With such self-control and peace, you can live there. Punna goes. The text says that in that one rains retreat he brought around five hundred men and five hundred women as lay followers, realized the three knowledges, and later attained final release. A word of care, though. This is a monk's training in patience, chosen freely, in a teaching about not clinging. It isn't advice to stay where someone hurts you. What anyone can borrow is the move itself: when something sharp lands, notice what didn't happen. They were rude, but they didn't shout. The email was curt, but it wasn't cruel. That's not pretending it was fine. It's refusing to let the worst version take over the mind.

Your line: at least they didn't. Patience here means seeing a hurt at its real size, never staying where you're harmed. Day five hundred ten.

511.title: Nandaka's full moon
511.hook: an elder teaches the nuns; they are satisfied like the full moon
511.howItsDone: The monastic rules ask the nuns' community to receive instruction (ovada) from the monks every half-month, and MN 146 shows one such teaching, given by questions and answers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: khanti, patience, and Punna's ladder of what didn't happen. Your line: at least they didn't.

Mahapajapati Gotami comes to the Buddha again, this time with five hundred nuns, asking him to teach them. In the hundred and forty-sixth discourse, the senior monks have been taking turns teaching the nuns. It's the turn of an elder named Nandaka, and he doesn't want to go. The discourse doesn't say why. The Buddha asks Ananda whose turn it is, hears the answer, and turns to Nandaka himself: teach the nuns, Nandaka. Give them a talk on the teaching. So Nandaka goes.
screen: `FIVE HUNDRED NUNS ASK TO BE TAUGHT.` → `IT'S NANDAKA'S TURN.` → `HE DOESN'T WANT TO GO.`

segments.voice: He teaches by asking. Sisters, is the eye permanent or impermanent? Impermanent, venerable sir. And what's impermanent, is it pain or ease? Pain, venerable sir. Is it fit to be called mine, me, my self? No, venerable sir. Through all six senses, their objects, and their kinds of knowing. Then three pictures. An oil lamp is burning: the oil, the wick and the flame all change. Would anyone say its light stays the same forever? A great tree: its roots, trunk, branches and leaves all change. Would its shadow be permanent? And a skilled butcher with a sharp knife, separating the hide from the flesh without cutting either: that's wisdom, slicing cleanly through what binds the mind. The nuns are pleased. But the Buddha sees they're glad, not yet fulfilled. Teach them again tomorrow, Nandaka, the same way. So he does. Then the Buddha uses the moon. On the fourteenth night, nobody looking up doubts it: the moon isn't full yet. That was the nuns after the first talk. On the fifteenth, nobody doubts either: the moon is full. That's the nuns after the second. The text says the least of the five hundred had entered the stream. Look back at the week: many names for a bowl, a stranger in a potter's shed, the truths expounded, a robe made by hand, a dying giver, Punna going west. And now a reluctant teacher, sent back a second time, until the moon was full.
screen: `TEACHING BY QUESTIONS` · `A LAMP, A TREE, A SHARP KNIFE` · `GLAD, BUT NOT YET FULFILLED` · `THE FOURTEENTH, THEN THE FIFTEENTH` · then, large: `THE MOON IS FULL.`
